candidate.derivedAnswer: A, PQRS is always a parallelogram
candidate.answerReason: The centers lie at intersections of the perpendicular bisectors of EA, EB, EC, and ED. These bisectors form two distinct parallel pairs, whose four intersections are P, Q, R, and S.

methods.label: Use the shared-segment perpendicular bisectors
methods.explanation:
The circumcenter of a triangle is equidistant from its vertices, so it lies on the perpendicular bisector of each side. This connects the centers of triangles sharing a segment.

For each vertex \(X\) among \(A,B,C,D\), let \(\ell_X\) be the perpendicular bisector of \(EX\). The four circumcenters are therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
P&=\ell_A\cap\ell_B,
&Q&=\ell_B\cap\ell_C,\\
R&=\ell_C\cap\ell_D,
&S&=\ell_D\cap\ell_A.
\end{aligned}
\]
Because \(ABCD\) is convex, \(E\) lies between \(A\) and \(C\), and between \(B\) and \(D\). Thus \(\ell_A\) and \(\ell_C\) are both perpendicular to \(AC\), so they are parallel. They are distinct because they meet \(AC\) at midpoints on opposite sides of \(E\). Likewise, \(\ell_B\) and \(\ell_D\) are distinct parallel lines perpendicular to \(BD\).

The two pairs have different directions because the diagonals \(AC\) and \(BD\) intersect. Their four intersections are consequently distinct. Now \(PQ\) lies on \(\ell_B\) and \(RS\) lies on \(\ell_D\), giving \(PQ\parallel RS\). Similarly, \(QR\) lies on \(\ell_C\) and \(SP\) lies on \(\ell_A\), giving \(QR\parallel SP\).

Both pairs of opposite sides are parallel, so \(PQRS\) is a parallelogram for every convex quadrilateral \(ABCD\), choice \(\mathrm{A}\).
